# Part 2 — Qualitative research {background-color="#7A003C"}

## Learning objectives (post-test portion)

By the end of the qualitative segment you will be able to:

- Choose among focus groups, IDIs, projective techniques, and observational methods for a research question
- Understand the rationale for projective methods (accessing unconscious motives)
- Plan a discussion guide for a focus group

::: {.notes}
Read out. Test-frazzled brains will need re-focusing. Read slowly,
give a moment for each objective to land.
:::

## Why qualitative?

Quantitative research answers *how many* and *by how much*.

Qualitative research answers *why*, *how*, and *what does it mean*.

Both are legitimate. Neither is a substitute for the other.

::: {.notes}
This isn't a rank ordering. Marketers who dismiss qualitative miss
motivational depth. Researchers who dismiss quantitative miss
generalisability. Serious insight work uses both.
:::

## When qualitative is right

- Exploratory phase (understand a phenomenon)
- Hypothesis generation
- Understanding motivations, feelings, meanings
- Studying rare or vulnerable populations
- Concept development (new product, new positioning)

Not for: quantifying, generalising to a population, causal claims.

::: {.notes}
Common misuse: treating 8 focus-group participants as representative
of a market. They're not. Use qualitative to develop hypotheses;
use quantitative to test them.
:::

## The main methods

- **Focus groups** — 6-10 participants, moderator-led discussion, 60-90 min
- **In-depth interviews (IDIs)** — 1 participant, 45-90 min, deep probing
- **Projective techniques** — indirect elicitation (ZMET, word association, drawing)
- **Observational / ethnographic** — watching behaviour in context

Each has strengths, weaknesses, cost profiles.

::: {.notes}
Discuss cost: focus group ~$10K per group, IDI ~$1.5K per interview,
ethnography ~$25K+ minimum. Projective is usually embedded in one of
the above. This shapes when each is used commercially.
:::

## Focus groups

**Strengths:**

- Group dynamic surfaces reactions ("that's a great idea!" "no wait, actually...")
- Cost-effective vs. IDIs for the same number of participants
- Live client observation possible

**Weaknesses:**

- Dominant participants skew discussion
- Social desirability bias
- Not suited for sensitive topics

::: {.notes}
Focus groups are workhorse commercial qualitative. Client-viewing
rooms are common - clients watch from behind one-way glass. This
raises ethics questions (consent to observed observation). Modern
online focus groups use platforms like Discuss.io.
:::

## In-depth interviews

**Strengths:**

- Deep probing, personal stories
- Suited for sensitive topics
- No group-dynamic contamination

**Weaknesses:**

- Expensive per participant
- Interviewer skill critical
- Longer analysis time

::: {.notes}
IDIs are the tool of choice for B2B research, professional
respondents, sensitive topics (health, finances, family). Recruit
carefully, prepare a detailed guide.
:::

## Projective techniques

Indirect ways to elicit unconscious motivations.

- **Word association:** "What comes to mind when you hear 'Starbucks'?"
- **Sentence completion:** "People who drink Maritime Roast are ___"
- **Third-person:** "What would your neighbour say about ___?"
- **Storytelling:** "Tell a story about a perfect morning with coffee"
- **ZMET (Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique):** participants collect images, moderator explores metaphors
- **Bubble drawings, personification, collages**

::: {.notes}
Projectives assume respondents can't or won't articulate their real
feelings directly. Especially useful for brand-image work,
premium/luxury categories, health/hygiene taboos.
:::

## Why projective? System 1 vs System 2

- **System 1** (Kahneman): fast, intuitive, emotional, non-conscious
- **System 2**: slow, deliberate, rational, conscious

Direct questioning taps System 2. Projective techniques bypass System 2 to access System 1 responses.

::: {.notes}
Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow. Consumer decisions are often
System 1 (impulse, habit, emotion). Yet questionnaires assume System
2 (rational reflection). Projectives are one workaround. Neuromarketing
is another (Wk 5 supplementary reading in MAI).
:::

## Observational / ethnographic

- **Non-participant observation:** watch shoppers in a store
- **Participant observation:** shop alongside them
- **Digital ethnography (netnography):** immerse in online communities
- **Home visits, shop-alongs, service journeys**

Studies actual behaviour rather than reported behaviour.

::: {.notes}
Kozinets coined netnography for online-community ethnography. Useful
for studying brand communities, product-use context, or subcultures.
Companies like Tribe (formerly Anthropology.io) specialise.
:::

## Digital qualitative

- Online focus groups (Discuss.io, Recollective)
- Mobile ethnography apps (dScout, Indeemo)
- Community platforms (Verto, Alida)
- Asynchronous discussion boards

Faster, cheaper, more diverse geography — but loses in-person nuance.

::: {.notes}
COVID accelerated digital qualitative adoption. Now standard. Ask
students: has anyone participated in an online focus group? What was
the experience?
:::

## Sample size for qualitative

- Focus groups: 3-5 groups per market segment
- IDIs: 8-15 per segment (until saturation)
- Ethnography: 4-8 units per segment

Rule: stop when new interviews stop revealing new themes ("saturation").

::: {.notes}
Saturation is the qualitative equivalent of sample size. Not
predetermined - determined during fieldwork. Sometimes you saturate
at 6, sometimes at 20. Budget must allow flex.
:::

## Analysing qualitative data

- **Transcribe** interviews / groups (verbatim if analysis is close)
- **Code** systematically (assign labels to segments)
- **Cluster** codes into themes
- **Interpret** themes in light of research questions
- **Report** with representative quotes + explanation

CAQDAS software: NVivo, ATLAS.ti, Dedoose, MAXQDA.

::: {.notes}
Coding is the analytic move that separates rigorous qualitative from
"we listened to the tape and here's our takeaway." Codes should be
defined, applied consistently, and inter-rater reliability checked
when possible.
:::

## Quotes vs. inference

- **Quotes** support findings with participant voice
- **Inference** synthesises across participants

Report should have both. Quotes without inference is journalism.
Inference without quotes is un-evidenced.

::: {.notes}
Show a sample qualitative findings slide if you have one. Good
qualitative reports read like a mix of ethnographic vignette and
analytic synthesis. Compare with academic qualitative writing (e.g.,
JCR papers with extended quote blocks).
:::

## R for qualitative — a small demo

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(readtext)
library(tidytext)

transcripts <- readtext("data/maritime_focus.txt")

tokens <- transcripts |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  anti_join(stop_words) |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(20)

tokens
```

R is illustrative for qualitative — real work uses CAQDAS.

A fuller worked version — word frequencies, a simple sentiment pass, and
a discussion of what text mining does and doesn't replace — is in
**`solutions-05.qmd`** in this session's folder.

::: {.notes}
30 seconds on this. Show output. Point out most-common words -
"coffee," "morning," "subscription." Text mining can complement, not
replace, human coding.
:::

# Part 3 — Focus-group workshop {background-color="#7A003C"}

## Workshop task (30 min)

Draft a **60-minute focus-group discussion guide** for:

*Maritime Roast wants to understand why 6-month subscribers churn. Design a guide for a focus group of 8 lapsed subscribers.*

Structure:

1. **Warm-up** (5 min): introductions, "tell us about your coffee habits"
2. **Main sections** (40 min): 3-4 topic areas
3. **Projective exercise** (10 min): one technique of your choice
4. **Wrap-up** (5 min): "if you could tell the CEO one thing..."

::: {.notes}
Small teams (3-4) of students. Circulate. Push for specificity - "we
would ask about the subscription experience" is not a question, it's
a topic. Guide should have actual question wording.
:::

## Discussion-guide tips

- Start broad ("tell us about..."), narrow gradually ("what specifically...")
- Use projective at a strategic point — usually mid-guide
- Prepare probes for each main question ("what makes you say that?")
- Practice moderator neutrality — no leading, no reacting

::: {.notes}
Moderating is a skill - takes years. Some students may go on to
moderate; most won't but will hire moderators. Knowing what a good
guide looks like helps you evaluate suppliers.
:::

## Share out (5 min)

Two or three teams present their guide highlights:

- The main question you're most excited about
- The projective exercise you chose and why

::: {.notes}
Time-box strictly - 2 min per team max. Point out one strong element
per team. Note common gaps: no consent statement, unclear projective,
too many warm-up questions.
:::

# Part 4 — Ethics thread (built into concept) {background-color="#7A003C"}

## Qualitative ethics

- **Participant vulnerability:** focus groups on sensitive topics can traumatise
- **Group dynamics coercion:** participants may over-share to fit in
- **Projective methods:** the line between insight and deception
- **Recording and consent:** all recordings need explicit consent
- **Anonymisation:** even quotes can identify (small industries, distinctive turns of phrase)

::: {.notes}
Sensitive-topic example: focus group of people with debt. Group
setting itself creates pressure to disclose. Use IDIs instead. For
projectives: never manipulate to gather data participants wouldn't
knowingly provide. Debrief after any technique that involved
concealment.
:::

## Debriefing

If a technique involved concealment (rare in commercial MR), debrief:

- Explain the true purpose
- Address any distress
- Allow withdrawal of data if requested
- Provide referrals if needed

::: {.notes}
Rare in commercial MR - most work is fully transparent. But if you
run a shop-along where the shopper doesn't know they're being
observed, that requires debrief. Better: get consent up front.
:::

# Part 5 — For your project {background-color="#7A003C"}

## What to think about

- Even quantitative projects benefit from **qualitative supplement**
- 3-5 informal interviews with people who know your target market can sharpen your quantitative design
- If time permits, include a "voice-of-customer" section in your project report

::: {.notes}
For a term-length project, real qualitative fieldwork is often
infeasible. But drafting a discussion guide as if you would run one
is a valuable exercise and can be part of the report methodology
section.
:::

## Draft a 3-question interview guide

For your project, sketch 3 questions you would ask a customer / user / decision-maker in your chosen decision context.

Not homework. Just a mental exercise this week.

::: {.notes}
Preview: some teams will find this exercise reveals blind spots in
their quantitative design. Others will realise their project doesn't
need qualitative at all. Both outcomes are useful.
:::
